draft.title: Types of data
card: data sorted into groups or labels. Nominal data has no natural order, such as eye colour. Ordinal data has a natural order, such as shirt size (small, medium, large).
data that is a count or a measurement. Discrete data is counted and takes separate values, such as the number of pets. Continuous data is measured and can take any value in a range, such as height.
A quick test: if you can do sensible arithmetic with the values, the data is numerical. Postcodes are numbers, but adding them means nothing, so they are categorical.
Categorical data suits a bar chart or sector graph. Numerical data suits a histogram or dot plot. A histogram is best for continuous data.
draft.remember: Categories name groups. Numbers count or measure. The type decides the display.

a.q: Students in a Year 11 class record the number of siblings each of them has. What type of data is this?
a.why: Siblings are counted, so the data is numerical and takes separate values: discrete. It is not continuous, because nobody has 1.5 siblings.

b.q: A café in Orange asks customers to rate its service as poor, fair, good or excellent. What type of data is this, and which display suits it?
b.why: The ratings are labels with a natural order, so the data is categorical and ordinal. Categorical data suits a bar chart. Nominal is wrong because the order of the ratings matters.
b.clue: Ratings are words, not counts, and they have an order.

problems.detail: "The type decides the display" is stronger than the card, which only says each type "suits" certain displays. It suggests there is one fixed display per type.
The clue states that the ratings are words, not counts, and that they have an order. That rules out the discrete and nominal options for the student, leaving only the choice of display to work out.
